snippet.title: Trying Gurgaon’s Most INSANE Street Food | The Urban Guide
snippet.description:
Girisha and Neeraj headed out to explore Gurgaon’s most insane street food, and the city completely surprised them with its incredible flavours and vibrant street culture.
Their first stop was the viral Kulcha Wala, known for serving soft, buttery kulchas paired with rich, flavourful chole that has taken social media by storm. Next, they tried Civil Lines wale Chole Bhature — famously known as Virat Kohli’s favourite —, and it absolutely lived up to the hype with its light, fluffy bhature and perfectly spiced chole.
The food trail continued with wheat momos, a healthier twist on Delhi-NCR’s beloved snack, stuffed generously and steamed to perfection. They then enjoyed some authentic Lucknowi kebabs, beautifully cooked with melt-in-the-mouth texture and aromatic spices.
To wrap up the experience, they sipped on refreshing coffee and ended the day with Golgappe, packed with tangy, spicy flavours that left them wanting more.

Let us know in the comments if we missed any iconic spots, and tell us what we should try in Part 2 of Gurgaon’s insane street food tour!

snippet.title: Jama Masjid delhi street food Tour Part 1 | Hilal Hotel, Babu bhai kebab, Aslam butter chicken!
snippet.description:
I travelled all the way from Pune to the heart of India's capital to spend 48 hours immersing myself in the rich history and even richer flavors of Old Delhi, right next to the iconic Jama Masjid.

Joined by my friend Lali (@LondonkiLali ) we explored the narrow lanes that are famous not only for their chaotic beauty but also for centuries-old food secrets. We ate breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the most iconic spots, and even found some hidden gems that completely blew us away!

🍽️ Our 24-Hours Food Journey Highlights:
 • The Royal Breakfast: We started at Hilal Hotel for the iconic Nalli Nihari, a slow-cooked dish that melted in the mouth and tasted like it came straight from the Mughal courts.
 • The Unexpected Kebab: We found Babu Bhai Kebab Wale and were shocked by how silky smooth and delicious the Chicken Kebab was—it’s simple, subtle, and an absolute must-try.
 • The Vegetarian Surprise: We stepped into Shyam Sweets for a sweet and savory experience: the Bedmi Puri and Sabzi (plus a secret addition of halwa!) that tasted just like Bhandara food, proving Old Delhi has something for everyone!
 • The Controversial Butter Chicken: We tried Aslam's, famous for literally bathing the chicken in butter, and then hunted down the late-night worker-favorite, Ya Allah Chala De Hotel, for a surprisingly delicious white-gravy butter chicken.
 • The Drink of Love: A stop for the universally loved, refreshing Mohabbat Ka Sharbat was essential

Address of the places: https://maps.app.goo.gl/Z8HqaYCQANXu6cPk8

snippet.title: Furniture DIY from a सब्ज़ी वाला Thela 😳 #shorts #homedecor #craft
snippet.description:
Furniture DIY from a सब्ज़ी वाला Thela 😳 #shorts #homedecor #craft

Waise toh i loveee experimenting in my DIYs but ye wala thodaaaa tricky tha 🤪

Here are all the details for this Thela Storage Desk -

➡️ Sabse pehle I replaced the big wheels with smaller ones so that you get enough space btw top and bottom rim jaha aap storage de sako. 

➡️ Now generally these carts don’t have a finished look so I had to cover the top portion with a 20 mm MDF board (directly used nails to fix them).

➡️ For storage, I made cubicles with a thin plywood aur dono ko attach kiya with screws (one in front and one at the back) I knew I was gonna have bamboo baskets in them so i’d say ki aap baskets ke measurements se 0.5-1 inch extra space rakhna. 

➡️ Next everything had to painted WHITE 🖌️ So pehle iron structure pe red oxide primer lagaya and then painted everything (including the plywood) with PU Enamel Paints. 

➡️ Once dried properly (about 24-36 hrs later) table top pe wooden wallpaper lagaya and for that real rustic feel I chose a wallpaper with grooving textures. 

➡️ Lastly made few alphabets for labelling using resin & silicon mould and bamboo baskets pe laga ke storage cubicles me slide in kar diye. That’s how our thela turned storage desk was ready 🥳

snippet.description:
Embark on an unforgettable Delhi to Jim Corbett road trip by car with us! 🚗🌲 We kicked off our journey from Le Meridien Gurgaon at 11 AM after a hearty breakfast. Our first stop was a COCO BP pump in Green Park, Delhi, to fuel up. We then cruised through Noida via the Barapullah flyover and gained speed, but hit a 3-hour traffic jam near Garh Mukteshwar. After finally getting back on track, we stopped at Bikanervala around 4 PM for a quick but satisfying meal of Chole Bhature and Lassi.

As we reached Moradabad, we left the main highway that heads to Lucknow and drove towards Nainital via Tanda and Bazpur. Navigating through the dark, we finally arrived at Kotabagh, nestled near Kaladhungi and Jim Corbett National Park.

snippet.description:
I traveled to Varanasi to meet the Dom caste - people who have been burning India's dead bodies for over 3,000 years. What I saw was unbelievable:

- They live right next to burning funeral pyres - over 100 bodies are cremated DAILY
- The same wood they use to burn bodies is also used to cook their food
- Their homes are filled with the smell of burning human flesh
- Many develop serious breathing problems from inhaling smoke their whole lives
- They celebrate a Masaan Holi using ashes from cremations

Despite river Ganga making them sick, these same people are working hard to save it from pollution.

According to local stories, Lord Shiva cursed their ancestors 6,000 years ago, and now they're stuck in this job for generations.

This video isn't just about death rituals - it's about real people living extraordinary lives that most of us can't imagine. You'll see families trying to maintain normal lives while surrounded by death every day. Despite everything, they keep their traditions alive.

Tell me in the comments which part of this video surprises you the most.

snippet.title: Best Old Delhi Sehri Night Food Walk | Champa Bread + Butter Jam Sheermal + Khajla, Pheni, Jalebi
snippet.description:
We began our sehri food walk in the historic lanes of Old Delhi, covering parts of Ballimaran, Daryaganj, and the areas around Jama Masjid. These neighbourhoods, steeped in centuries of tradition, come alive in a unique way during Ramzan, especially in the quiet, anticipatory hours before dawn.

Next, we stopped by Khan Omelette Corner. Their Khan Special Omelette was a buttery, cheesy affair, rich in calories but undeniably delicious. This indulgent dish is quite the local favourite, especially for those looking to fuel up before a long day of fasting.

Our next stop was Islam Bhai’s night food stall, a humble but vital eatery that runs late into the night. It caters mostly to workers and labourers, offering hearty meals at pocket-friendly prices. The setup was simple, but the energy and sense of community were palpable.

We then made our way to Shamsi Milk Shop, where we had a glass of hot milk. Thick, slightly sweet, and served in a no-nonsense way, it offered warmth and comfort amidst the night’s quiet chill.

Although we didn’t eat at Mohd. Sagheer Nahari Wale, we were struck by the sizeable crowd gathered outside. The popularity of their nihari spoke volumes, and while we didn’t try it, its reputation clearly draws people in even at such early hours.

At Al Haj Bakery, we met the genial owner who walked us through their offerings and the bakery’s history. It was a nostalgic place, where we tried rusk and a few other baked treats. The sense of pride and tradition infused every word he shared.

Flora Bakery was another delightful discovery. The owner introduced us to a wide range of fresh breads and sheermal, all traditionally consumed during sehri. But the highlight was their champa milk bread — soft, fragrant, and rich with stories that added layers of meaning to every bite.

Ameer Sweet House showcased some of their special Ramzan-time delights. We saw and sampled items like meetha samosa, paneer jalebi, khajla, and feni. The display was a feast for the senses, and the variety of textures and flavours reflected the festive spirit of the season.

At Mohd. Shakeel Milk Shop, we ordered a bowl of milk and had it the local way — with champa bread dipped in, accompanied by khajla, feni, and feeki jalebi. The place was buzzing with energy and locals enjoying their early morning ritual.

We ended our walk at Wazeeruddin Tea Stall, where we had a warm cup of coffee. This old establishment carries the charm of a bygone era, and its patrons seem to return not just for the brew, but for a sense of familiarity and comfort. 

As we wrapped up the tour, we came across a sehri wale — a man who walks through the lanes, calling out the names of residents to wake them up for sehri. It was a touching reminder of an old tradition that still thrives in pockets of the city, rooted in community bonds and a deep sense of care.

Although we didn’t eat at Mohd. Sagheer Nahari Wale, we were struck by the sizeable crowd gathered outside. The popularity of their nihari spoke volumes, and while we didn’t try it, its reputation clearly draws people in even at such early hours.

At Al Haj Bakery, we met the genial owner who walked us through their offerings and the bakery’s history. It was a nostalgic place, where we tried rusk and a few other baked treats. The sense of pride and tradition infused every word he shared.

Flora Bakery was another delightful discovery. The owner introduced us to a wide range of fresh breads and sheermal, all traditionally consumed during sehri. But the highlight was their champa milk bread — soft, fragrant, and rich with stories that added layers of meaning to every bite.

Ameer Sweet House showcased some of their special Ramzan-time delights. We saw and sampled items like meetha samosa, paneer jalebi, khajla, and feni. The display was a feast for the senses, and the variety of textures and flavours reflected the festive spirit of the season.

At Mohd. Shakeel Milk Shop, we ordered a bowl of milk and had it the local way — with champa bread dipped in, accompanied by khajla, feni, and feeki jalebi. The place was buzzing with energy and locals enjoying their early morning ritual.

We ended our walk at Wazeeruddin Tea Stall, where we had a warm cup of coffee. This old establishment carries the charm of a bygone era, and its patrons seem to return not just for the brew, but for a sense of familiarity and comfort. 

As we wrapped up the tour, we came across a sehri wale — a man who walks through the lanes, calling out the names of residents to wake them up for sehri. It was a touching reminder of an old tradition that still thrives in pockets of the city, rooted in community bonds and a deep sense of care.

Haryanvi rapper Dhanda Nyoliwala delivers a compelling performance, weaving relatable narratives with his signature cadence. He's joined by Xvir Grewal, whose melodic interpretation adds another layer of depth to the exploration of love and loss. The production is a vibrant fusion of modern sounds and traditional Haryanvi instrumentation, featuring the distinctive textures of the Deru, Bugchu and Ghada, creating a sonic landscape that is both familiar and refreshingly new

Delhi to Lucknow by Road: A Journey Across North India
The road journey from Delhi to Lucknow is a fascinating experience that offers a unique opportunity to explore the heart of North India. Spanning a distance of around 550-600 kilometers (depending on the route), the drive typically takes anywhere between 10 to 12 hours, making it a long but enriching trip. The road itself is an essential part of India's vast transportation network, connecting the national capital to the capital of Uttar Pradesh. Along the way, travelers pass through diverse landscapes, bustling towns, and historical sites that showcase India's rich culture and heritage.

Route Options for the Journey
There is primary route for this road trip

Via Yamuna Expressway and Agra-Lucknow Expressway: Another alternative is taking the Yamuna Expressway from Delhi, which leads to Agra. From Agra, drivers can proceed via the Agra-Lucknow Expressway, a state-of-the-art highway that connects Agra to Lucknow. This route, though slightly longer, provides a faster and more comfortable driving experience, especially with less congestion and a well-maintained highway.

Preparing for the Trip
Before setting out, it's essential to prepare adequately for the long road trip. Check your vehicle's condition—ensure that it is well-maintained, has enough fuel, and is stocked with essential supplies like water, snacks, and first aid kits. Since it’s a long journey, it’s advisable to take regular breaks to rest, stretch, and recharge. Also, familiarize yourself with key landmarks, rest areas, and refueling stations along the route to make the trip as smooth as possible.

Highlights of the Journey
The drive from Delhi to Lucknow offers a glimpse into the heart of India. Here are some of the key highlights you can expect along the way:

Delhi to Ghaziabad: As you leave Delhi, the first major city you’ll encounter is Ghaziabad. Located just across the border from Delhi, this bustling city marks the start of your journey through Uttar Pradesh. Ghaziabad is known for its industrial areas, and while it's a busy city, it offers good infrastructure and ample food and fuel options for travelers. This stretch is relatively smooth, and you'll soon find yourself on the NH44 heading toward Meerut.

Meerut and Muzaffarnagar: As you drive further on NH44, you'll pass through Meerut, a historic city that is a hub for education and commerce. Meerut is known for its role in the First War of Indian Independence in 1857. After Meerut, the road continues toward Muzaffarnagar, a district that offers rural views and small towns. The scenery here begins to shift from the urban hustle of Delhi to the quieter and more peaceful outskirts of Uttar Pradesh.

The Yamuna River and Etawah: Continuing on, you will reach the area near the Yamuna River. As you cross bridges over this historic river, you might catch glimpses of rural life along the banks. Further along, you'll approach Etawah, a city of significant historical importance. It is also known for its proximity to the Chambal River, famous for the Chambal ravines. This area has a unique charm with its mix of rural life and modern development.

Agra and the Agra-Lucknow Expressway: If you choose the Yamuna Expressway route, you’ll encounter the city of Agra, home to one of the Seven Wonders of the World—the Taj Mahal. Agra is a great place to stop for a brief break, where you can visit the Taj, the Agra Fort, or just explore the bustling markets. After Agra, the Agra-Lucknow Expressway beckons. This expressway is one of the most modern and well-maintained roads in India, making it a smooth and fast route toward Lucknow.

Fatehpur Sikri: Whether you're on NH44 or the Agra-Lucknow Expressway, you’ll pass near Fatehpur Sikri, another UNESCO World Heritage site. Fatehpur Sikri is a historical city that was once the capital of the Mughal Empire under Emperor Akbar. It’s a site full of historical significance and provides an excellent chance to take a detour and explore Mughal architecture.

Rural Landscape and Small Towns: As you approach the outskirts of Lucknow, the landscape gradually becomes more rural. Small towns, lush fields, and agricultural landscapes come into view, showcasing the beauty of the Indian countryside. The journey’s final leg offers a transition from the bustling urban areas of Delhi and Agra to the more serene atmosphere of Lucknow, known for its old-world charm and modern development.

Arrival in Lucknow
Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh, is a city known for its rich cultural heritage, Mughal architecture, and Nawabi cuisine. Upon arrival, you'll be welcomed by an elegant blend of history and modernity. The city is famous for its vibrant markets, exquisite historical monuments, and delicious food, including kebabs, biryanis, and the famous Lucknawi chikan work.
